raw_case_text:
A 73-year-old male farmer presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of fever (38.3 C), fatigue, chest tightness, and myalgia. On presentation, the patient was alert, with regular heart rate and normal blood pressure. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 39 C and gastrocnemius muscle pain impairing walking. Laboratory tests revealed thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 48 x 109/L. Renal function tests revealed an elevated creatinine level (237 umol/L). CPK was 791 U/L (normal range 50-310 U/L) and CK-MB was 26 U/L (normal range <25 U/L). The C-reactive protein level was 160.44 mg/dL, and his hemoglobin level, white blood cell count and live function test was normal. Initial computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed multiple infections in both lungs (Figure 1A).
The patient was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam at 13:55. At 15:22, the patient developed unconsciousness, fever, rigor, increasing tachycardia with a heart rate of 190 beats/min, hypotension (82/42 mmHg), tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 36 breaths/min, and hypoxia with peripheral capillary oxygen saturation of 78%. Intubation for respiratory support was immediately performed, and bloody sputum was aspirated during suctioning. Despite fluid therapy, the patient's blood pressure remained low, and norepinephrine was administered to maintain blood pressure. A repeat chest CT showed diffuse bilateral exudation that had worsened after previous imaging (Figure 1B). His C-reactive protein level was elevated to 200.22 mg/L. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a PaO2 of 49.4 mm Hg and an oxygenation index of 80.98 with an oxygen concentration of 61%. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed dark red, bloody sputum in the airways, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) samples collected from the airways and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid revealed Leptospira interrogans. Further history revealed that the patient had been exposed to and consumed raw river water before the onset of symptoms. The diagnosis of leptospirosis was made based on the patient's history, fiberoptic bronchoscopy results, CT manifestations, laboratory tests, and clinical presentation.
Additionally, the patient's disease state worsened dramatically after the administration of piperacillin tazobactam, with respiratory failure and septic shock. Pulmonary CT showed diffuse exudative lesions (examined 2.5 h after treatment), deemed JHR caused by penicillin treatment. The penicillin dose was reduced, and 40 mg methylprednisolone was administered every 12 h. When the conditions improved, the penicillin dose was adjusted to 400,000 units every 8 h for 2 weeks and subsequently discontinued. On the 7th day after onset, pulmonary CT showed an absorption of the lesion. Methylprednisolone was reduced after 2 weeks to 30 mg every 12 h for 3 days, 20 mg every 12 h for 3 days, and 20 mg daily for 3 days until discontinued.
After 2 weeks of treatment, the patient's temperature gradually decreased to normal, myalgia resolved, blood gas analysis showed a gradual increase in oxygenation index from 80.98 to 342.42 and 369.7 to normal, and chest imaging improved significantly (Figure 1C); norepinephrine was discontinued, and the endotracheal tube was removed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old male farmer presenting with a 4-day history of fever, fatigue, chest tightness, and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 73-year-old male farmer presented with a 4-day history of fever (38.3 C), fatigue, chest tightness, and severe myalgias. He was admitted for community-acquired pneumonia and initiated on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam. Within 90 minutes of the first antibiotic infusion, he experienced acute clinical deterioration with sudden unconsciousness, fever, rigors, extreme tachycardia (heart rate 190 beats/min), shock (blood pressure 82/42 mmHg), tachypnea, and severe hypoxemia (SpO2 78%), consistent with a severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Emergency endotracheal intubation revealed massive bloody airway secretions, and repeat CT demonstrated diffuse bilateral alveolar exudation/pulmonary hemorrhage. With aggressive mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, steroids, and targeted penicillin dosing, his respiratory and renal failure resolved, allowing extubation and complete recovery.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation as a farmer. Epidemiological exposure: Had contact with and drank unboiled, raw river water prior to symptom onset. No other prior medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports chest tightness, fatigue, fever, and severe lower extremity muscle pain.

objective.physical_examination:
Admission vitals: Temperature 39.0 C, regular heart rate, normal blood pressure, alert. Severe gastrocnemius muscle tenderness significantly impairing ambulation.
Post-antibiotic infusion deterioration (15:22): Temperature spiked, unconscious, heart rate 190 beats/min, blood pressure 82/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths/min, SpO2 78% on room air. Endotracheal suctioning revealed gross dark red, bloody sputum.
objective.routine_investigations:
Admission labs: Platelet count 48 x 10^9/L, serum creatinine 237 umol/L, CPK 791 U/L (normal 50-310 U/L), CK-MB 26 U/L (normal <25 U/L), CRP 160.44 mg/dL; normal hemoglobin, normal WBC count, and normal liver function tests.
Post-deterioration labs: CRP increased to 200.22 mg/L.
Arterial blood gas (post-intubation): PaO2 49.4 mmHg, PaO2/FiO2 (oxygenation index) 80.98 on FiO2 0.61. During recovery: PaO2/FiO2 index progressively improved from 80.98 to 342.42 and 369.7.
objective.advanced_workup:
Initial chest CT: Multiple bilateral pulmonary infections/infiltrates.
Repeat chest CT (2.5 hours post-infusion): Marked worsening with diffuse bilateral exudative lesions consistent with severe alveolar hemorrhage.
Chest CT (day 7 and week 2): Significant interval absorption and resolution of exudative lesions.
Fiberoptic bronchoscopy: Dark red bloody secretions filling the tracheobronchial tree.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed severe leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans) complicated by diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, thrombocytopenia, and a severe penicillin-induced Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR) manifesting as hyperpyrexia, shock, and sudden respiratory collapse. Confirmed by mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and airway secretions identifying Leptospira interrogans. Raw river water consumption was identified as the source of exposure.
Plan & Outcome: Immediate endotracheal intubation, lung-protective mechanical ventilation, aggressive fluid resuscitation, and intravenous norepinephrine. Following the JHR, piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped, intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg q12h) was initiated, and low-dose penicillin G was started at 400,000 units q8h for 2 weeks. Methylprednisolone was gradually tapered (30 mg q12h for 3 days, 20 mg q12h for 3 days, 20 mg daily for 3 days, then stopped). The patient made a complete clinical recovery, was successfully extubated, weaned off norepinephrine, and discharged.
